newsitem.title: CROATIA: FEATURE - High interest rates frustrate Croatian middle class.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - High interest rates frustrate Croatian middle class.

text.p: Kamilo Zlatic is about to buy the first home he can afford for his family in the provincial town of Pozega after working for 15 years.

The 40-year-old Croatian, who is married to a dentist and has two children, works as the transport manager for a foreign company. He has saved two thirds of a very attractive purchase price of 60,000 German marks ($40,000) and borrowed the rest from a bank.

In Croatia the usual recipe is: scrape what you have saved with some difficulty over the years, borrow as much as possible from relatives and friends and, finally, get the rest from a bank if you must. Wrong way round, one might say.

But in a country without institutions such as Western-style building societies, where only a few banks grant mortgages at up to 11 percent a year and require four guarantors and 30-50 percent collateral, it is the only way.

Zlatic is actually at the top of the ladder of middle-class citizens struggling to make ends meet on meagre salaries. They can ill afford real estate or other investments in a stifling transitional economy after decades under Yugoslav communism.
Typically, they earn just over 2,000 kuna (about $400) a month on average, live with an older generation until parents or grandparents die, and perhaps have a second-hand car.
FOREIGN BANK LOANS NOT EASY TO GET
Although foreign banks are opening in Croatia almost every month and more external loans are raised constantly, these are not readily available for the needs of most ordinary people.
Small entrepreneurs and even middle-sized firms that could form the backbone of an economy scarred by a 1991-95 war with Serbs after independence from Yugoslavia are no exception.
"No one will give big enough long-term credits to new production enterprises," complained Mario Vucur, a young furniture manufacturer, eager to expand his prosperous but relatively small business.
"You have to be a well-known client to get a loan and then, I certainly could not pay 5,000-10,000 German marks ($3,326 to $6,651) a month in interest," he added.

Analysts say commercial banks must boost their support of private enterprises while not reducing much needed funding of state-owned industry to prevent it from being pushed over the edge by mounting debt and war devastation.

They also say that for most branches of Croatia's economy to grow after a three-year period of stability, banks will have to increase long-term funding and offer more reasonable rates than the average 18.7 percent charged in September.
With a low inflation rate of 3.2 percent in the first 10 months of 1996, high real interest rates are widely criticised as a key obstacle to speedy economic recovery.
"Reducing lending rates through reform of the banking sector remains of great importance to future growth," said a research paper published by the Nomura Research Institute last month.

Some bankers admit privately that they could easily trim the rates further after recent modest cuts by a few percentage points, but they appear reluctant to be the first to give up their handsome profit margins.

However, the largest banks, emerging from decades under the communist centrally-planned economy with a pile of uncollected debts and huge burden of risk provisions, complain they cannot increase loans and substantially reduce rates.
They are now striving to attract more long-term deposits, albeit at slightly lower rates than the over 10 percent they were running at not long ago.
EFFORTS TO MAKE CAPITAL CHEAPER
They are also making efforts to make capital cheaper.
After the government gave cash injections to three ailing banks this year, inter-bank rates plunged to around nine percent this summer from more than 30 percent.

Although the average bank lending rate also dropped some eight percentage points from 26.6 percent in January, government and central bank officials say the scope for further cuts is far from exhausted.

"By the end of this year, rates could go down another one to two percentage points," said central bank chief analyst Velimir Sonje, envisaging the downward trend to last through 1997 as efforts to overhaul the ailing banking sector continue.
This process will soon include the largest bank, the ailing state-controlled Privredna Banka Zagreb.
Its rehabilitation is expected to lead to further cuts in money market rates and interest charged to the public sector, the bank's main customer base.

Sonje said banks also had to widen the share of relatively risk-free loans to citizens from the current 7.5 percent of their total assets, while cutting down on doubtful credits to heavily indebted enterprises and the state.
To help this, the central bank vowed to continue easing the reserve requirement, which gradually fell to around 35 percent from over 40 percent on kuna deposits at the beginning of 1996.
It also cut the discount rate to 6.5 from 8.5 percent and the Lombard emergency borrowing rate to 11 from 18 percent.

But it insisted banks must do their bit by cutting down on staff hired during the communist era, slashing operating costs and improving overall efficiency to help narrow their wide spreads, now more than 10 percent.
"The increasing competition by foreign banks will soon press our banks to lower all interest rates," Sonje added. ($1=1.5034 Mark)
